newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Scania says new series dents profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Scania says new series dents profit.

text.p: Swedish truck and bus maker Scania on Thursday reported that profits dropped 39 percent in the first nine months of the year, blaming the stronger crown, a restructuring programme and the cost of its new 4-series trucks.

Scania posted a profit of 2.14 billion crowns ($324.4 million) after financial items, down from 3.51 billion in the same 1995 period. Sales totalled 24.57 billion crowns for the period compared with 25.44 billion.
If sales had been adjusted for the strength of the Swedish crown, they would have risen two percent, Scania said.
The stronger currency was also to blame for 720 million crowns of the nine-month profit slide, but that was not the only reason, Scania said.
Costs incurred in the changeover in European production to the group's new 4-series trucks from the older 3-series had also been a serious drain.
"The costs of the production transition to the 4-series was 450 million crowns (by the end of the third quarter), of which 300 million was taken during the third quarter," Scania said in a statement.
The company said these costs would persist into the fourth quarter, which would also be hit to the tune of 300 million crowns by a programme to cut the workforce.
The profit came in well short of market expectations of 2.65 billion crowns, and by the close Scania shares were nine crowns lower at 167, down from 174.50 before the result was released.
Analyst Peter Malmqvist of Sweden's Aragon brokerage said the transition costs had exceeded consensus expectations but that they should not be as heavy in the fourth quarter.
He called the results disappointing, especially the third quarter, and said they could scare off small investors in the short term.
"But 175 crowns could be a reasonable level for the share by year-end," Malmqvist said.

Foreningsbanken automotive analyst Jan Ihrfelt said the company's main problem was its operating margin, which fell to 9.9 percent for the first three quarters of the year from 15.3 percent in the same 1995 period.
Scania, billed as the world's most profitable truckmaker thanks to an operating margin which stayed steadfastly above 12 percent for many years, may not see those levels again, Ihrfelt said.
"I think it's a thing of the past. We had a very different currency situation in Sweden at that time."
Scania said new orders for the period fell to 26,539 trucks from 29,563. Invoicing fell to 28,799 trucks from 29,156.
On the plus side, market share in western Europe rose slightly to 15.4 percent from 14.4 percent, while in Brazil, market share increased to 37.5 percent from 33.9 percent.

Britain remains Scania's largest single market. Scania truck registrations increased to 4,487 from 4,105 in the same 1995 period, and Scania improved its market share to 18.2 percent from 16.7 percent.
Total order bookings for buses fell to 2,501 units from 3,328. Sales totalled 3,073 buses compared with 3,143.

Scania returned to the stock market in April after investment company Investor AB spun off a majority of the shares in the company in what it then called the world's largest public share offering. ($1=6.596 Swedish Crown)
